title: Character Encoding
tagline: From ASCII's 128 characters to emoji grapheme clusters — why text is harder than it looks.

sections.content:
When you type a letter on a keyboard and see it appear on the screen, a remarkable translation happens invisibly: the key press is converted to a number, that number is stored in memory as bits, and the display system converts that number back to a visual glyph. The rules for this translation are called a **character encoding**. Get the encoding wrong at any step — receiving, storing, transmitting, or rendering — and readable text becomes a cascade of garbled symbols, a phenomenon so common in the early web that it earned its own name: **mojibake** (文字化け, Japanese for 'character transformation').

Character encoding is not just a historical curiosity. It is the reason why an HTTP header says `Content-Type: text/html; charset=UTF-8`, why Python 3 made `str` Unicode by default (breaking millions of Python 2 scripts), why a tweet can contain emoji but has a character limit that depends on how you count, and why two engineers reading the same string can disagree on how many 'characters' it contains. Every engineer who handles text — which is to say, every engineer — needs to understand encoding at a mechanical level.

This article traces the history and mechanics of character encoding from its simplest form (ASCII's 128-character table) through the internationalization crisis that spawned Unicode, into the encoding formats that represent Unicode in bytes (UTF-8, UTF-16, UTF-32), and finally into the genuinely subtle territory of surrogate pairs, grapheme clusters, and the Byte Order Mark. Along the way we will calculate byte lengths by hand and verify every claim in JavaScript.

The central insight to hold in mind throughout: **a character encoding is a mapping between abstract characters (what humans see) and concrete byte sequences (what computers store)**. The character and its encoding are different things — conflating them is the source of most encoding bugs.

sections.title: Codebook, Language, and Transmission Format
sections.content:
Imagine you and a colleague want to send messages using only numbers, but you both need to represent symbols from different languages. You first agree on a **codebook** — a lookup table mapping every symbol you might write to a unique number. Then you agree on a **transmission format** — whether to send each number in 1 byte, 2 bytes, or some variable-length shorthand. The codebook is the character set; the transmission format is the encoding scheme.

ASCII was the first widely adopted codebook for computing: 128 entries, numbers 0–127, covering the Latin alphabet, digits, punctuation, and control codes. It worked perfectly for English. But when the rest of the world wanted to compute in French, Russian, Arabic, Chinese, or emoji, the codebook had to be vastly expanded — and the transmission format had to be redesigned to encode the new codebook efficiently without wasting memory.

Think of Unicode as an enormous, universal codebook shared by all humans. It has over a million entries (called code points), one for every character in every language ever written. UTF-8, UTF-16, and UTF-32 are three different transmission formats for the same codebook. They are interchangeable in principle but differ in efficiency, byte alignment, and compatibility with older systems. Choosing the wrong format — or misreading one format as another — is mojibake.

sections.title: ASCII: The First Universal Codebook
sections.content:
**ASCII** (American Standard Code for Information Interchange, 1963) assigns the integers 0–127 to 128 characters using 7 bits. The mapping is fixed and permanent — identical today as in 1963.

**The layout (key groups):**
- **0–31 and 127:** Control characters (non-printable). Tab = 9, linefeed (newline) = 10, carriage return = 13, escape = 27, null = 0 (string terminator in C).
- **32:** Space.
- **33–47 and 58–64 and 91–96 and 123–126:** Punctuation and symbols: `! " # $ % & ' ( ) * + , - . / : ; < = > ? @ [ \ ] ^ _ \`` { | } ~`
- **48–57:** Digits `0`–`9`. Crucially, `'0'` = 48, `'9'` = 57. Subtracting 48 from the code converts an ASCII digit character to its numeric value.
- **65–90:** Uppercase `A`–`Z`. `'A'` = 65, `'Z'` = 90.
- **97–122:** Lowercase `a`–`z`. `'a'` = 97, `'z'` = 122.

**The uppercase/lowercase pattern:** Lowercase = uppercase + 32. In binary, `'A'` is `01000001` and `'a'` is `01100001` — they differ only in bit 5 (value 32). XOR-ing any ASCII letter with 32 toggles its case. This is why old C code for `toLower(c)` was sometimes written as `c | 32` and `toUpper(c)` as `c & ~32`.

**Why 7 bits?** The 8th bit was reserved for **parity** in early serial transmission — a simple error-detection mechanism. A byte was 8 bits, but only 7 carried data, giving 128 code points. Enough for English, not for anything else.

**The CR/LF divergence:** ASCII separately defined carriage return (CR = 13, `\r`) and linefeed (LF = 10, `\n`). When teletype terminals ended a line, they needed both: CR moved the print head left, LF advanced the paper. Unix chose LF-only (`\n`). Windows (following CP/M and DOS) chose CR+LF (`\r\n`). Old Mac OS used CR-only (`\r`). This three-way split still breaks text files when copied across platforms, and is why `git` has a `core.autocrlf` setting.

sections.title: Extended ASCII and the Encoding Tower of Babel
sections.content:
Once hardware settled on 8-bit bytes and parity was no longer stored in the high bit, that 8th bit became available for 128 more code points (128–255). Every vendor and standards body filled those slots differently, creating dozens of competing **extended ASCII** encodings.

**ISO 8859-1 (Latin-1):** The most common Western European extension. Adds `é` (0xE9 = 233), `ñ` (0xF1), `ü` (0xFC), copyright sign © (0xA9). Used by HTTP/1.0 as the default for `text/html`.

**Windows-1252 (CP1252):** Microsoft's variant of Latin-1. Adds printable characters in the 0x80–0x9F range that ISO 8859-1 left as unused control codes, including the Euro sign `€` at 0x80 (but Unicode puts `€` at U+20AC — a mismatch that corrupts files when the encoding is misidentified).

**ISO 8859-5:** Replaces code points 0xA0–0xFF with Cyrillic characters for Russian, Bulgarian, Serbian. Incompatible with Latin-1.

**Shift-JIS:** Japanese encoding using 1 byte for ASCII and 2 bytes for Japanese characters, with complex lead-byte rules. EUC-JP is an alternative Japanese encoding. They are mutually incompatible.

**GB2312 / GBK / GB18030:** Simplified Chinese encodings, progressively expanding. Big5 covers Traditional Chinese. All incompatible with each other and with Japanese encodings.

**The crisis:** By the late 1980s, a text file sent from Tokyo to Paris to Moscow was garbled at every hop. Email clients displayed mojibake. HTML pages had to specify `charset=` in meta tags and hope browsers respected it. An unlabeled 8-bit text file was fundamentally ambiguous. This was the encoding Tower of Babel, and it was the direct motivation for Unicode.

sections.title: Unicode: One Codebook for All Human Writing
sections.content:
**Unicode** (first published 1991, maintained by the Unicode Consortium) assigns a unique integer — called a **code point** — to every character in every script used by humans. As of Unicode 15.1 (2023), there are 149,813 defined characters with room for over 1.1 million total (the full range is U+0000 to U+10FFFF, spanning 1,114,112 possible code points).

**Code point notation:** Written as `U+` followed by 4–6 uppercase hex digits. `U+0041` = `A`, `U+00E9` = `é`, `U+4E2D` = `中` (zhōng, 'middle/China'), `U+1F600` = `😀`.

**Unicode planes:** The 1.1 million code points are organized into 17 planes of 65,536 code points each (0x10000 code points per plane).
- **Plane 0: Basic Multilingual Plane (BMP)** — U+0000 to U+FFFF. Contains virtually all modern scripts in everyday use: Latin, Greek, Cyrillic, Arabic, Hebrew, Devanagari, Thai, Hangul, and the CJK Unified Ideographs block (the most common Chinese/Japanese/Korean characters). The vast majority of text in everyday computing lives here.
- **Plane 1: Supplementary Multilingual Plane (SMP)** — U+10000 to U+1FFFF. Historic scripts (Linear B, cuneiform, Egyptian hieroglyphs), musical notation, math alphanumerics, and most emoji (including `😀` at U+1F600 and all the newer emoji).
- **Plane 2: Supplementary Ideographic Plane (SIP)** — U+20000 to U+2FFFF. Rare CJK characters not included in the BMP.
- **Plane 14:** Language tags and variation selectors.
- **Planes 15–16:** Private Use Areas — code points that applications can define for their own purposes without conflicting with Unicode assignments.

**Code points vs. characters vs. grapheme clusters:** A **code point** is a number in the Unicode table. A **grapheme cluster** is what a user perceives as a single character on screen. Some grapheme clusters are composed of multiple code points: a base character plus one or more **combining marks**. The letter `é` can be U+00E9 (precomposed form) OR `e` (U+0065) + combining acute accent (U+0301) — both render identically. Emoji like `👩‍🔬` (woman scientist) are a single grapheme cluster composed of three code points joined by a Zero Width Joiner. This multiplicity is why 'string length' is ambiguous without specifying the unit.

sections.title: UTF-8: Variable-Length Encoding and Why It Won the Internet
sections.content:
**UTF-8** (Unicode Transformation Format, 8-bit units) is a variable-length encoding that represents each code point as 1, 2, 3, or 4 bytes. Designed by Ken Thompson and Rob Pike in 1992 on a napkin in a New Jersey diner, it has become the dominant encoding on the web (over 97% of web pages as of 2024).

**The encoding rules** are determined entirely by the code point's numeric range:

| Code point range | Bytes used | Byte patterns | Available bits |
|---|---|---|---|
| U+0000 – U+007F | 1 | `0xxxxxxx` | 7 bits |
| U+0080 – U+07FF | 2 | `110xxxxx 10xxxxxx` | 11 bits |
| U+0800 – U+FFFF | 3 | `1110xxxx 10xxxxxx 10xxxxxx` | 16 bits |
| U+10000 – U+10FFFF | 4 | `11110xxx 10xxxxxx 10xxxxxx 10xxxxxx` | 21 bits |

The `x` bits carry the actual code point value. Continuation bytes always start with `10`, making them immediately distinguishable from leading bytes. A leading byte starting with `0` is a 1-byte sequence; `110` starts a 2-byte sequence; `1110` starts a 3-byte sequence; `11110` starts a 4-byte sequence.

**Worked examples (all verified in Node.js):**

`A` (U+0041 = 65 = `01000001₂`): code point fits in 7 bits → **1 byte**: `0 1000001` = `0x41`.

`é` (U+00E9 = 233 = `11101001₂`): needs 8 bits → **2 bytes**: fill template `110xxxxx 10xxxxxx` with bits `00011 101001` → `11000011 10101001` = `0xC3 0xA9`.

`中` (U+4E2D = 19,501 = `100111000101101₂`): needs 15 bits → **3 bytes**: fill `1110xxxx 10xxxxxx 10xxxxxx` with bits `0100 111000 101101` → `11100100 10111000 10101101` = `0xE4 0xB8 0xAD`.

`😀` (U+1F600 = 128,512 = `11111011000000000₂`): needs 17 bits → **4 bytes**: fill `11110xxx 10xxxxxx 10xxxxxx 10xxxxxx` → `0xF0 0x9F 0x98 0x80`.

**Why UTF-8 won:**
1. **ASCII backward compatibility.** Any byte in 0x00–0x7F is interpreted identically to ASCII. Existing ASCII files and C strings work without modification. This was the decisive factor for adoption.
2. **Self-synchronizing.** If you start reading in the middle of a UTF-8 byte stream, you can find the start of the current character by scanning backward for a byte that does not begin with `10`. Shift-JIS cannot do this.
3. **No endianness issues.** UTF-8 is a byte stream, not a sequence of multi-byte words. There is no ambiguity about byte order (see BOM section).
4. **Compact for Latin text.** English, French, Spanish, Portuguese, and other Latin-based scripts use 1 byte per character. CJK text uses 3 bytes (UTF-16 uses 2 for BMP CJK, but UTF-8's other advantages outweigh this for most use cases).
5. **Simple error detection.** Invalid byte sequences are easily detected: a lone `10xxxxxx` byte without a preceding leading byte is invalid.

sections.label: UTF-8 Byte Lengths
sections.explanation: All outputs verified in Node.js 18. A=1, é=2, 中=3, 😀=4 UTF-8 bytes as computed from the encoding rules. The three-length demonstration shows why 'string length' is ambiguous: the same emoji is length 2 (UTF-16 code units), 1 (code point), or 4 (UTF-8 bytes). The combining character example shows that visually identical strings can differ at the byte level — normalize before comparing.

sections.title: UTF-16: Surrogate Pairs and the JavaScript String Surprise
sections.content:
**UTF-16** encodes Unicode code points as sequences of 16-bit **code units** (2 bytes each). For BMP code points (U+0000–U+FFFF), one code unit suffices. For supplementary code points (U+10000–U+10FFFF), UTF-16 uses a **surrogate pair**: two code units from specially reserved ranges.

**Why surrogate pairs exist:** The BMP has 65,536 slots. When Unicode was designed, the range U+D800–U+DFFF (2,048 code points) was permanently reserved — never assigned to any character — specifically to serve as surrogate code unit values in UTF-16. This makes surrogates unambiguously identifiable in a byte stream.

**The surrogate ranges:**
- High surrogates: U+D800–U+DBFF (1,024 values)
- Low surrogates: U+DC00–U+DFFF (1,024 values)
- Together: 1,024 × 1,024 = 1,048,576 pairs — enough for all supplementary planes.

**Encoding algorithm** for supplementary code point `cp` (U+10000 and above):
1. `cp' = cp − 0x10000` (subtract base to get 20-bit offset, range 0–0xFFFFF)
2. High surrogate = `0xD800 + (cp' >> 10)` (top 10 bits of cp')
3. Low surrogate = `0xDC00 + (cp' & 0x3FF)` (bottom 10 bits of cp')

**Worked example — 😀 (U+1F600):**
- `cp' = 0x1F600 − 0x10000 = 0xF600`
- High = `0xD800 + (0xF600 >> 10)` = `0xD800 + 0x3D` = `0xD83D`
- Low = `0xDC00 + (0xF600 & 0x3FF)` = `0xDC00 + 0x200` = `0xDE00`
- UTF-16: `[0xD83D, 0xDE00]` — verified: `'😀'.charCodeAt(0).toString(16)` = `'d83d'`

**JavaScript's hidden UTF-16:** ECMAScript specifies that `string` is a sequence of **UTF-16 code units**. Consequences:
- `'😀'.length === 2` — two code units, not one character
- `'😀'[0]` returns `'\uD83D'` — a lone high surrogate with no visual representation
- `[...'😀'].length === 1` — the spread operator iterates *code points*, handling surrogates correctly
- `'😀'.codePointAt(0) === 0x1F600` — `codePointAt` reconstructs the full code point from a surrogate pair
- `'😀'.charCodeAt(0) === 0xD83D` — `charCodeAt` gives the raw UTF-16 code unit

**UTF-16 users:** Windows API (wchar_t), Java `char`, JavaScript/ECMAScript, C# `char`, Swift `String.UTF16View`, .NET `System.String`. All share the surrogate-pair gotcha for supplementary characters.

sections.title: UTF-32: Simplicity at a Cost
sections.content:
**UTF-32** is the simplest possible Unicode encoding: every code point uses exactly 4 bytes (32 bits). U+0041 (`A`) is stored as `0x00000041`. U+1F600 (`😀`) is stored as `0x0001F600`. No variable-length encoding, no surrogate pairs.

**Advantages:**
- **Constant-time random access:** The nth code point starts at byte offset `n × 4`. This gives O(1) indexing by code point number, which variable-length encodings cannot provide.
- **No surrogate pairs:** Every 4-byte unit is exactly one code point, no special cases.
- **Simple implementation:** A naïve implementation is straightforward.

**Disadvantages:**
- **4× larger than UTF-8 for ASCII text.** An English novel would quadruple in file size.
- **Not ASCII-compatible.** The `A` character in UTF-32 LE is the 4 bytes `41 00 00 00`, which contains null bytes that terminate C-style strings.
- **Byte-order ambiguity** — needs BOM or explicit declaration of UTF-32LE vs UTF-32BE.
- **Rare in practice.** Files and network protocols almost never use UTF-32. It appears mainly as an internal in-memory representation.

Python 3 uses a clever **compact internal representation**: strings containing only Latin-1 characters use 1 byte per code point; strings containing only BMP characters use 2 bytes; strings containing supplementary characters use 4 bytes. This is UTF-32 for the last case but more compact otherwise.

**Important caveat:** Even UTF-32 does not solve the grapheme cluster problem. A flag emoji `🇺🇸` is two code points (U+1F1FA + U+1F1F8) — two 4-byte units in UTF-32 — but one visual character. O(1) code point access ≠ O(1) grapheme cluster access.

sections.title: The Byte Order Mark (BOM) and Endianness
sections.content:
When UTF-16 or UTF-32 data is stored as bytes, there is a fundamental ambiguity: does the most-significant byte of each code unit come first (big-endian) or last (little-endian)? The 2-byte UTF-16 code unit `0x004E` can be stored as `00 4E` (UTF-16BE) or `4E 00` (UTF-16LE). On x86 systems (little-endian), UTF-16LE is native. On network protocols (big-endian), UTF-16BE is traditional.

**The Byte Order Mark (BOM)** solves this by placing the Unicode character U+FEFF at the very start of the file. When the reader sees `FE FF` as the first two bytes, it knows the file is UTF-16BE (because U+FEFF in big-endian is `FE FF`). When it sees `FF FE`, it knows UTF-16LE. For UTF-32: `00 00 FE FF` = UTF-32BE; `FF FE 00 00` = UTF-32LE.

**UTF-8 BOM (EF BB BF):** UTF-8 has no byte-order ambiguity. However, the UTF-8 encoding of U+FEFF is `EF BB BF`, and some tools (historically Microsoft Notepad) prepend these 3 bytes to UTF-8 files as a format indicator. This optional marker causes real problems:
- PHP source files with a BOM fail to set HTTP headers because the response body starts with 3 invisible bytes before `<?php`.
- Python `open('file', 'r')` does not strip the BOM by default; `open('file', 'r', encoding='utf-8-sig')` does.
- Unix `cat`, `grep`, and `wc` commands include the BOM in their output.

**Best practice for new code:** Use UTF-8 without BOM everywhere. Only use BOM when specifically interoperating with tools that require it (some Excel workflows require a UTF-8 BOM to recognize UTF-8 CSV files).

sections.label: Surrogate Pairs & Grapheme Clusters
sections.explanation: All outputs verified in Node.js 18. The flag 🇺🇸 is 2 code points but 4 UTF-16 code units; it is 1 grapheme cluster. The woman scientist emoji is 3 code points (woman + ZWJ + microscope) but 5 UTF-16 code units and 1 grapheme cluster. Only Intl.Segmenter correctly counts all three as 1 visible character.

sections.title: Mojibake: When Encodings Collide
sections.content:
**Mojibake** is what appears on screen when text encoded in one scheme is decoded using a different scheme. It is the most visible symptom of encoding confusion, and historically one of the most common bugs in international software.

**The mechanics:** UTF-8 encodes `é` (U+00E9) as two bytes: `0xC3 0xA9`. If those two bytes are read as Latin-1 (ISO 8859-1), which maps each byte 0x00–0xFF to a single code point, they decode as `Ã` (0xC3) + `©` (0xA9) — the famous `Ã©` mojibake pattern.

**Common mojibake fingerprints and their causes:**
| Mojibake | Original | Encoding mismatch |
|---|---|---|
| `Ã©` | `é` | UTF-8 read as Latin-1 |
| `â€™` | `'` (right single quote, U+2019) | UTF-8 read as Windows-1252 |
| `Ã¼` | `ü` | UTF-8 read as Latin-1 |
| `ï¿½` | replacement character U+FFFD | UTF-8 bytes were truncated |
| `??` or boxes | CJK characters | CJK encoding read as ASCII |

**Real-world mojibake scenarios:**
1. **MySQL `utf8` vs `utf8mb4`:** MySQL's historic `utf8` type only stores 3-byte UTF-8 sequences (BMP only). Storing emoji (4-byte sequences) either fails silently or raises a truncation error. The fix: `ALTER TABLE t CONVERT TO CHARACTER SET utf8mb4 COLLATE utf8mb4_unicode_ci`. Django, Rails, and WordPress all shipped with this bug in their default configurations until corrected in their documentation.
2. **Windows Notepad (before 2019):** Opened files without BOM using the system ANSI code page (CP1252 in Western Europe). UTF-8 files without BOM displayed mojibake until Microsoft changed the default in 2019.
3. **Email clients:** An email body sent in UTF-8 without `Content-Type: charset=utf-8` in the header may be displayed by the client using the system locale — Latin-1, CP1252, or Shift-JIS — producing garbled text.
4. **Python 2 implicit decoding:** Concatenating a `str` (bytes) and `unicode` object in Python 2 triggered implicit ASCII decoding of the `str`, raising `UnicodeDecodeError` when the bytes included non-ASCII values.

**Prevention principles:** Declare encoding explicitly at every I/O boundary. Validate incoming bytes are well-formed UTF-8 before processing. Use UTF-8 as the single encoding for all new systems. In databases, use `utf8mb4` (MySQL) or the default `UTF8` (PostgreSQL). In HTTP, always include `charset=utf-8` in `Content-Type`.

sections.title: Emoji, Grapheme Clusters, and the Length Problem in Practice
sections.content:
Modern emoji make the grapheme cluster problem unavoidable. A single visible emoji may be composed of many code points, which in turn become many bytes in any encoding. Code that uses `.length` to limit user input (Twitter's character count, database varchar limits, SMS segmentation) must choose a unit carefully.

**Types of complex emoji and their composition:**

**1. Basic supplementary emoji:** `😀` = U+1F600 = 1 code point = 2 UTF-16 code units = 4 UTF-8 bytes = 1 grapheme.

**2. Emoji + skin tone modifier:** `👋🏽` = U+1F44B (waving hand) + U+1F3FD (medium skin tone modifier) = 2 code points = 4 UTF-16 code units = 8 UTF-8 bytes = 1 grapheme. The 5 skin tone modifiers are U+1F3FB–U+1F3FF (Fitzpatrick scale).

**3. Regional indicator sequences (flags):** `🇺🇸` = U+1F1FA + U+1F1F8 = 2 code points = 4 UTF-16 code units = 8 UTF-8 bytes = 1 grapheme. The 26 regional indicators (U+1F1E6 'A' through U+1F1FF 'Z') combine in pairs to form country flags.

**4. ZWJ sequences (Zero Width Joiner):** `👩‍🔬` (woman scientist) = U+1F469 (woman) + U+200D (ZWJ) + U+1F52C (microscope) = 3 code points = 5 UTF-16 code units = 11 UTF-8 bytes = 1 grapheme. `👨‍👩‍👧` (family) = 5 code points, 8 UTF-16 code units, 18 UTF-8 bytes. Platforms that do not support the ZWJ sequence render each code point separately.

**5. Variation selectors:** `♥️` (red heart) = U+2665 (black heart suit) + U+FE0F (variation selector 16, 'emoji presentation') = 2 code points but displays as one emoji. Without the selector, `♥` renders as a text symbol.

**The correct API for each measurement:**
| Goal | JavaScript API | Example for 😀 |
|---|---|---|
| UTF-16 code units | `str.length` | 2 |
| Unicode code points | `[...str].length` | 1 |
| UTF-8 bytes | `new TextEncoder().encode(str).length` | 4 |
| Grapheme clusters (user chars) | `[...new Intl.Segmenter().segment(str)].length` | 1 |

For character limits in user interfaces (tweet length, bio limits, SMS), use grapheme clusters. For database storage limits (VARCHAR byte lengths), use UTF-8 byte count. For JS string manipulation (slice, indexOf), remember UTF-16 code units are the native unit but surrogate pairs must be handled carefully — use code-point-aware methods where available.

**Unicode Normalization Forms** matter whenever you compare or store user-generated text. The same visible character can have multiple byte representations:

- **NFC (Canonical Decomposition + Canonical Composition):** Decomposes then recomposes. `é` stored as U+00E9 (precomposed). Most common on the web and in databases — use this by default.
- **NFD (Canonical Decomposition):** Fully decomposes to base + combining marks. `é` stored as `e` + U+0301. macOS HFS+ filesystem stores filenames in NFD, causing `é` in a filename to differ from `é` in a Python string on Linux.
- **NFKC / NFKD:** Add compatibility decomposition. Converts `ﬁ` (ligature) → `fi`, `²` → `2`, full-width `Ａ` → `A`. Useful for search normalization and username validation.

Always call `string.normalize('NFC')` before storing user text or comparing strings for equality. Failing to normalize is a common source of 'duplicate username' bugs where users register with `é` and `é` (visually identical, different bytes).

**Interview and production checklist for character encoding:**

1. **Always declare UTF-8 explicitly** at every I/O boundary: HTTP `Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8`, file open with explicit encoding, database connection charset.
2. **Use `utf8mb4` in MySQL/MariaDB**, not `utf8` — the historical `utf8` type silently drops 4-byte emoji and supplementary characters.
3. **Never use `.length` for user-visible character limits.** Use `Intl.Segmenter` for grapheme clusters, or at minimum `[...str].length` for code points.
4. **Normalize before comparing or storing user strings:** `str.normalize('NFC')`.
5. **`'😀'.length === 2` in JavaScript** — always, because JS strings are UTF-16 code units. This surprises many developers and is a common interview question.
6. **Mojibake diagnosis shortcut:** `Ã©` for `é` = UTF-8 read as Latin-1. `â€™` for `'` = UTF-8 read as Windows-1252. `?` or boxes = wrong encoding, no fallback.
7. **Avoid UTF-8 BOM** in new files — many Unix tools and HTTP parsers do not strip it, causing invisible bugs.

items: ASCII maps 128 characters (0–127) to 7 bits; uppercase letters start at 65, lowercase at 97 — they differ only by bit 5 (value 32). ASCII's CR vs LF distinction still causes line-ending compatibility issues today.

Extended ASCII encodings (Latin-1, Windows-1252, Shift-JIS, GB2312, etc.) filled the 8th bit with region-specific characters, creating hundreds of mutually incompatible encodings and widespread mojibake.
Unicode assigns a unique code point (U+0000 to U+10FFFF) to every character in all human scripts; organized into 17 planes of 65,536 each, with most everyday text in Plane 0 (BMP).

UTF-8 uses 1–4 bytes per code point with self-synchronizing prefix bits; backward-compatible with ASCII; won the web (97%+ adoption) due to ASCII compatibility, no byte-order issues, and compactness for Latin text.

JavaScript strings are UTF-16 code units: emoji in the supplementary planes (U+10000+) need a surrogate pair (2 code units), making `'😀'.length === 2`. Use `[...str]` for code points and `Intl.Segmenter` for grapheme clusters.

Mojibake occurs when bytes encoded in one scheme are decoded with another (e.g., UTF-8 bytes for 'é' decoded as Latin-1 give 'Ã©'). Prevention: always label and enforce encoding at every I/O boundary.

A grapheme cluster is one user-perceived character; it may span multiple code points (skin tone modifiers, ZWJ sequences like 👩‍🔬, regional indicator pairs like 🇺🇸). Only `Intl.Segmenter` counts them correctly — use it for any user-facing character limit.

quiz.question: What is the ASCII code point of the uppercase letter 'A'?
quiz.explanation: 'A' is ASCII 65 (decimal). Lowercase 'a' is 97 = 65 + 32. Digits start at 48 ('0' = 48). The value 41 is hexadecimal for 65 (0x41 = 65 in decimal) — a common confusion, but the question asks for the decimal code point.

quiz.question: How many bytes does the UTF-8 encoding of the CJK character '中' (U+4E2D) require?
options: 1 byte
2 bytes
3 bytes
4 bytes
quiz.explanation: U+4E2D falls in the range U+0800–U+FFFF, which requires 3 UTF-8 bytes (pattern: 1110xxxx 10xxxxxx 10xxxxxx). Verified: new TextEncoder().encode('中').length === 3. The bytes are 0xE4 0xB8 0xAD.

quiz.question: In JavaScript, what does '😀'.length return and why?
options: 1, because it is one visible character
4, because emoji are stored as 4 UTF-8 bytes
2, because JavaScript strings are UTF-16 code units and this emoji needs a surrogate pair
3, because U+1F600 has 5 hex digits
quiz.explanation: JavaScript strings are sequences of UTF-16 code units. U+1F600 is above U+FFFF (in the supplementary plane), so it requires two UTF-16 code units called a surrogate pair: 0xD83D (high) and 0xDE00 (low). Therefore .length === 2. To get the code point count, use [...'😀'].length === 1.

quiz.question: What is mojibake?
options: A type of Unicode normalization for Japanese text
Garbled text that results from decoding bytes with the wrong character encoding
A Japanese character encoding standard used before Unicode
A BOM sequence prepended to UTF-16 files
quiz.explanation: Mojibake (文字化け, 'character transformation') is garbled text caused by decoding bytes using a different encoding than was used to write them. Classic example: UTF-8 bytes for 'é' (0xC3 0xA9) decoded as Latin-1 produce 'Ã©'.

quiz.question: Which UTF encoding is most space-efficient for a file containing only ASCII text?
options: UTF-32
UTF-16 LE
UTF-8
All use the same number of bytes for ASCII
quiz.explanation: UTF-8 uses exactly 1 byte per character for U+0000–U+007F (ASCII range), identical to plain ASCII. UTF-16 always uses at least 2 bytes per character. UTF-32 always uses 4 bytes. For ASCII-only text, UTF-8 is 2–4× more compact than the alternatives.

quiz.question: What is the purpose of a surrogate pair in UTF-16?
options: To detect byte order (endianness) of the file
To encode code points above U+FFFF using two 16-bit code units drawn from reserved ranges
To mark the beginning of a UTF-16 encoded stream
To represent combining diacritical marks like accents
quiz.explanation: A single UTF-16 code unit can only represent U+0000–U+FFFF. For supplementary code points (U+10000–U+10FFFF), UTF-16 uses a surrogate pair: a high surrogate (U+D800–U+DBFF) followed by a low surrogate (U+DC00–U+DFFF). These ranges are permanently reserved in Unicode for this purpose.

quiz.question: Two strings look identical on screen: 'é' (U+00E9) and 'e' + combining acute accent (U+0065 U+0301). What is true?
options: They are equal with === because JavaScript compares visual appearance
They are not equal with ===, but become equal after .normalize('NFC')
They are equal with === because both are valid UTF-8
Only UTF-32 encoding can distinguish them
quiz.explanation: The precomposed U+00E9 and the decomposed sequence U+0065+U+0301 are different byte sequences, so === returns false. Unicode normalization canonicalizes both to the same form: .normalize('NFC') converts both to precomposed U+00E9, making them === equal.

quiz.question: When is including a UTF-8 Byte Order Mark (BOM, bytes 0xEF 0xBB 0xBF) problematic?
options: Always — it is never permitted in UTF-8 by the standard
When tools or HTTP parsers include it as part of the content, causing invisible extra bytes at the start
Only when the file contains CJK characters
Only when the file is larger than 64KB
quiz.explanation: The UTF-8 BOM (0xEF 0xBB 0xBF, the UTF-8 encoding of U+FEFF) is optional in UTF-8. It causes problems when tools include it as visible content: PHP files with a BOM fail to send HTTP headers (response starts with BOM before <?php), Python reads it as data unless encoding='utf-8-sig' is specified.

quiz.question: What is the correct JavaScript API to count user-visible characters (grapheme clusters) in a string containing emoji?
options: str.length
[...str].length
[...new Intl.Segmenter().segment(str)].length
new TextEncoder().encode(str).length
quiz.explanation: str.length counts UTF-16 code units. [...str].length counts code points. TextEncoder gives UTF-8 byte count. Only Intl.Segmenter iterates grapheme clusters — what users perceive as single characters. It correctly handles ZWJ sequences (👩‍🔬), regional indicator pairs (🇺🇸), and skin tone modifiers.

quiz.question: Why should MySQL databases use 'utf8mb4' instead of 'utf8' for Unicode support?
options: utf8mb4 is faster due to 4-byte memory alignment
MySQL's 'utf8' only supports 3-byte UTF-8 sequences (BMP only) and silently drops 4-byte emoji
utf8mb4 supports more collations for alphabetical sorting
MySQL 'utf8' stores in Latin-1 internally
quiz.explanation: MySQL's historically misnamed 'utf8' character set only stores UTF-8 sequences up to 3 bytes, covering only BMP code points (U+0000–U+FFFF). Characters requiring 4 UTF-8 bytes — including all emoji like 😀 (U+1F600) — are silently truncated or cause an error. The correct type is 'utf8mb4', which supports the full UTF-8 range including supplementary planes.
